def: A compulsion to put objects in the mouth and explore them orally. It is a feature of Kluver-Bucy syndrome, caused by bilateral amygdala damage.
Caused by medical treatment or a clinician's actions rather than the underlying disease, such as Wernicke encephalopathy precipitated by giving glucose before thiamine.
Neuronal death from excessive stimulation by glutamate, which overactivates NMDA receptors and lets in toxic amounts of calcium. It is implicated in stroke and Huntington disease.
Located above the tentorium cerebelli, the dural sheet separating the cerebrum from the cerebellum. Most adult primary brain tumors are supratentorial; most childhood ones are infratentorial.
Increased colonic motility triggered by food entering the stomach, which often prompts a bowel movement soon after a meal.
A muscle at the junction of the pharynx and esophagus that forms the upper esophageal sphincter. A weak area just above it is where a Zenker diverticulum forms.
Relating to the junction of the ileum and cecum, or to the ileocolic artery supplying it. The ileocecal region is the typical site of intussusception and Crohn disease.
A brand of guaiac-based fecal occult blood test that detects hidden blood in stool, used for colorectal cancer screening.
Associated with stones. Calculous cholecystitis is gallbladder inflammation caused by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct, the usual cause.
A dopamine pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the prefrontal cortex. Reduced activity is linked to the negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
A butterfly-shaped skull base bone containing the sella turcica, which holds the pituitary, and the sphenoid sinus. Structures of the cavernous sinus lie beside it.
The period after a seizure, marked by confusion, drowsiness and sometimes transient weakness (Todd paralysis). Absence seizures have none.
Areas of skin supplied by sensory fibers of a single spinal nerve root, used to localize spinal cord and root lesions. For example, S2-S4 supply the perineum.
High CSF protein with a normal cell count, a classic finding in Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Drainage from the ear, such as pus in otitis externa or cholesteatoma, or cerebrospinal fluid after a basilar skull fracture.
A mature ego defense in which unacceptable impulses are redirected into socially acceptable activity, such as channeling aggression into sports.
A fixed false belief that others are plotting to harm or follow the patient, the most common delusion in schizophrenia.
A viral life cycle in which phage DNA integrates into the bacterial genome and replicates silently. Prophages can carry toxin genes, such as the strep erythrogenic toxin.
Antiepileptic and neuropathic pain drugs such as gabapentin and pregabalin that bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing neurotransmitter release.
Paralytic drugs such as rocuronium that competitively block acetylcholine at the nicotinic receptor of the neuromuscular junction. Sugammadex or neostigmine reverses them.
Fraternal twins from two separate eggs fertilized by two sperm. They share about half of their genes, which twin concordance studies compare against identical twins.
A branch of L1-L2 that supplies the cremaster muscle (efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex) and skin of the upper thigh and scrotum or labia.
Coating of a pathogen with molecules such as IgG or C3b so phagocytes can recognize and engulf it more easily.
A graft between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins, which is not rejected.
Disease of several endocrine glands at once. IPEX is immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked, caused by FOXP3 mutation.
A raised, scaly, round red skin patch with scarring and follicular plugging, seen in discoid lupus and as a lupus diagnostic criterion.
A family of inflammatory arthritides of the spine and sacroiliac joints that are HLA-B27 associated and rheumatoid factor negative, such as ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis.
A coarse, thickened, lion-like facial appearance, seen in lepromatous leprosy and also in Paget disease of bone with skull overgrowth.
Thickening of skin with accentuated skin lines from chronic rubbing or scratching, as in long-standing atopic dermatitis.
A genus of gram-positive anaerobic skin bacteria formerly called Propionibacterium. C. acnes contributes to acne and can infect prosthetic joints.
A direct thrombin inhibitor used as an anticoagulant during percutaneous coronary intervention and for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
A slender bony projection of the temporal bone (or of the radius or ulna) serving as an attachment for muscles and ligaments.
An extended-spectrum penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, sold as Timentin, covering Pseudomonas and many gram-negatives.
A selective progesterone receptor modulator used as emergency contraception up to 5 days after intercourse.
Esophageal narrowing that mimics achalasia but is caused by another process such as a tumor at the gastroesophageal junction.
Removal of a polyp, usually endoscopically during colonoscopy.
A JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor used for myelofibrosis and polycythemia vera.
An incomplete fracture in children in which one side of the bone cortex breaks and the other bends, like a young green twig.
Relating to the palms and soles, as in palmoplantar erythema from capecitabine hand-foot syndrome.
Whether a population of cells all descended from a single progenitor cell, as in a tumor. X-inactivation patterns can show clonality in women.
A ball of Aspergillus hyphae growing in a preexisting lung cavity (for example after tuberculosis), causing hemoptysis.
Occurring in skin folds where surfaces rub together, such as the axilla, groin or under the breasts, a typical site of candidal rash.
A molecule that binds metal ions tightly so they can be excreted, such as deferoxamine for iron and dimercaprol for lead.
Organisms that require oxygen to grow, using it as the final electron acceptor. Obligate aerobes include Pseudomonas, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Nocardia.
Able to kill bacterial spores. Autoclaving and some chemicals such as glutaraldehyde are sporicidal; alcohol and quaternary ammonium compounds are not.
A streptogramin antibiotic given with quinupristin to treat vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium. They bind the 50S ribosome.
A streptogramin antibiotic given with dalfopristin to treat vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium. They bind the 50S ribosome.
A long-acting rifamycin used with isoniazid in short-course tuberculosis regimens. It induces cytochrome P450 enzymes.
A single-dose 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial that clears Plasmodium vivax hypnozoites; it causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Agents that loosen and shed the outer skin layer, such as salicylic acid and urea, used for scaling disorders and warts.
A kidney brush-border enzyme that degrades imipenem, which is why it is given with cilastatin, an inhibitor of the enzyme.
Inspection of the back of the eye (retina, optic disc, vessels) with an ophthalmoscope.
A topical antihistamine used as eye drops for allergic conjunctivitis and as a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis.
Inspection of the ear canal and tympanic membrane using an otoscope.
Having increased blood flow or engorged vessels, giving a red appearance.
A non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor for HIV. It can cause vivid dreams and CNS effects and is teratogenic.
Shedding or peeling of the outer layer of skin, as in scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease and hand-foot syndrome.
Insertion of a drug between stacked DNA base pairs, distorting the helix. Doxorubicin and dactinomycin work in this way.
Scratch marks where the skin surface has been broken by scratching, seen in pruritus, scabies and methamphetamine use.
A VMAT2 inhibitor used to treat tardive dyskinesia by reducing presynaptic dopamine storage.
Dormant liver-stage forms of Plasmodium vivax and ovale that cause relapse; primaquine or tafenoquine eliminates them.
Protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium that cause malaria, transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes.
